job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today we are looking at Arithmetic Progressions. Remember, an AP is a list of numbers where the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant. Rohan, if I have 10, 7, 4, 1, what is the common difference? Rohan: Since 10 minus 7 is 3, the difference is 3. Teacher: Not quite. You must subtract the earlier term from the later one, so 7 minus 10 gives a common difference of -3. Priya: Does that mean the common difference must always be positive? Teacher: No, it can be negative or zero. Now, consider the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16. Is this an AP? Priya: Yes, because it grows by a rule. Teacher: Actually, no. An AP must have a constant difference between every single pair of consecutive terms. Here, 4-2 is 2, but 8-4 is 4. Since the differences are not the same, it is not an AP. Finally, to find the nth term, we use the formula a_n = a + (n-1)d. If you want to find the 10th term of an AP starting with 3 and a difference of 4, you calculate 3 + (10-1) times 4, which is 39. Do not confuse the term value with the position n; they are distinct concepts.

items.evidence: You must subtract the earlier term from the later one, so 7 minus 10 gives a common difference of -3.
items.q: Meena finds the common difference of 20, 15, 10, 5. Which working is right?
items.explain: Subtract the earlier term from the later one: 15 - 20 = -5.

wrong.why: subtracts the later term from the earlier one
adds terms instead of finding their difference

items.evidence: No, it can be negative or zero.
items.q: What is the common difference of the AP 6, 6, 6, 6?
options: Zero, as each term equals the next
Positive, as a difference cannot be zero
None, as an AP must keep increasing
Six, as every term has the value six
items.explain: Every term equals the next, so the difference is zero, and a common difference can be zero.

wrong.why: thinks the difference can never be zero
thinks an AP must keep increasing
confuses the term value with the difference

items.evidence: An AP must have a constant difference between every single pair of consecutive terms.
items.q: A list has gaps 3, 3, 5 between neighbours. A student checks only the first two gaps. What goes wrong?
options: The list fails, since the last gap differs
The list passes, since the first gaps match
The list passes, since it grows by a rule
The list fails, since every gap must be 3
items.explain: An AP needs the same difference between every pair of consecutive terms, so the last gap matters too.

wrong.why: thinks two matching gaps are enough
thinks growing by a rule makes an AP
thinks the common difference must be 3

items.evidence: If you want to find the 10th term of an AP starting with 3 and a difference of 4, you calculate 3 + (10-1) times 4, which is 39.
items.q: An AP starts at 5 with common difference 2. Which working gives its 8th term?
items.explain: The nth term is a + (n-1)d, so the 8th term is 5 + 7 × 2 = 19.

wrong.why: uses a + nd instead of a + (n-1)d
mixes up the order of operations

items.evidence: Do not confuse the term value with the position n; they are distinct concepts.
items.q: In the AP 4, 9, 14, 19, what is a_3?
options: 3, because a_n and n are the same
19, because the term is a + nd
items.explain: The 3 is the position; the third term is 14, a different thing from n.

wrong.why: thinks the nth term equals n
uses a + nd and gets the fourth term
picks the common difference instead of the term
